::: {.why}
The technique that turns a hard calculation into a one-line answer, and the one where the conditions matter because the classic doubling strategy violates exactly one of them.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Solve six martingale problems under a clock, identifying the martingale before computing anything.
- State the optional stopping conditions and say which one a doubling strategy violates.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [40 min]{.task-min} Forty minutes, six problems. The hard part is finding the martingale, so for each one write down the candidate before proceeding. For a biased walk the martingale is an exponential of the position, and recognising that once is worth more than solving three problems.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Work the doubling strategy carefully: it appears to guarantee a profit, and it fails because the stopping time is not bounded and the wealth is not, which is a violation of the boundedness condition. Say it out loud in the form an interviewer wants, which names the condition and then names the real-world thing that enforces it.
:::
:::

- [Durrett — Probability: Theory and Examples (author's free 5th ed. draft)](https://services.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf) [textbook]{.res-kind}
- [Grinstead & Snell — Introduction to Probability (free PDF)](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf) [textbook]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A scored six-problem session with the martingale identified in writing before each solution.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Doubling after every loss appears to guarantee a profit. Name the optional stopping condition it violates and what enforces that condition in reality.
:::
